George Orwell, pen name of Eric Arthur Blair. The English author and political essayist whose dystopian novels warned against totalitarian power and the manipulation of language and thought. His work merged speculative extrapolation with urgent moral witness, making him a touchstone for dissent and intellectual freedom. Orwell's 1984, published in 1949, presents the bleakest vision of state surveillance and control, depicting a totalitarian state of perpetual war, omniscient surveillance, and linguistic reengineering through doublethink, newspeak, and the Ministry of Truth. He created the concept of Thought Police and telescreens—surveillance apparatus that merged menace and the mundane in a way that seemed prophetic decades later. His earlier work, Animal Farm, published in 1945, stood as an allegory of the Russian Revolution in which revolutionary ideals are betrayed by their own inheritors, particularly the pig Napoleon representing Stalin. Orwell coined or popularized the terms doublethink, thoughtcrime, and Big Brother, which entered public discourse and persist as touchstones for critiquing power. Throughout his career as journalist, essayist, and political commentator, he grounded his speculative fiction in lived experience of fascism, colonialism, and communist bureaucracy. His entire oeuvre emphasizes that totalitarianism is not a mere political system but a colonization of thought itself.
